cases.sql: UPDATE users SET status = 'active' WHERE id = 42;
cases.rationale: The UPDATE includes an explicit WHERE clause with a row-limiting condition (id = 42) that restricts the affected rows to a single intended record.

cases.sql: UPDATE orders SET shipped = TRUE WHERE order_date < '2024-01-01' AND status = 'pending';
cases.rationale: The UPDATE has a WHERE clause with meaningful conditions (order_date and status) that limit the affected rows to a specific subset of pending orders from before 2024.

cases.sql: UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.1 WHERE category_id = 5 AND discontinued = FALSE;
cases.rationale: The UPDATE contains a WHERE clause with explicit conditions (category_id = 5 and discontinued = FALSE) that restrict the update to a bounded subset of products.

cases.sql: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 1000 WHERE department_id IN (10, 20) AND hire_date > '2020-01-01';
cases.rationale: The UPDATE has a WHERE clause with row-limiting conditions (department_id IN (...) and hire_date > ...) that clearly bound the affected rows to a specific group of employees.

cases.sql: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 123 AND balance >= 100;
cases.rationale: The UPDATE includes an explicit WHERE clause with conditions (account_id = 123 and balance >= 100) that restrict the affected rows to a single intended account.
The UPDATE has no WHERE clause at all, so it applies to every row in the table and is an unbounded update.

cases.sql: UPDATE orders SET shipped = TRUE WHERE 1=1;
cases.rationale: The UPDATE has a WHERE clause, but the condition 1=1 is always true and does not restrict the affected rows, resulting in an unbounded update.

cases.sql: UPDATE products SET price = 0 WHERE id = id;
cases.rationale: The WHERE clause contains only the always-true predicate id = id, which matches every row and provides no meaningful restriction on the update.

cases.sql: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE TRUE;
cases.rationale: The WHERE clause uses the always-true literal TRUE, so it does not limit the affected rows and the UPDATE is effectively unbounded.
The WHERE clause contains only an always-true constant comparison ('a' = 'a') and does not restrict the affected rows, violating the bounded update requirement.
